sections.b: 3 Maccabees names God's care with the Greek philosophers' word pronoia, "providence" (3 Maccabees 4:21; 5:30). It works first through ordinary things: the king's register cannot be finished because the papyrus and pens run out (3 Maccabees 4:20). Then God works on the king himself, sending a deep sleep (3 Maccabees 5:11–12) and putting "a forgetting" into his mind (3 Maccabees 5:28). Only at the end does he act openly, by angels (3 Maccabees 6:18). The pattern recalls Esther, where God is never named but the king's sleepless night turns everything (Esther 6:1), and Proverbs: "the king's heart lies in the LORD's hand" (Proverbs 21:1).

sections.h: The two angels in the hippodrome
sections.b: In 3 Maccabees God "opened the gates of heaven," and two glorious angels came down, "visible to everyone except the Jews" (3 Maccabees 6:18). They bind the army with terror and turn the elephants on the king's troops (3 Maccabees 6:19–21). The scene recalls the two young men who flog Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3:26 and the angel who struck Sennacherib's camp (2 Kings 19:35), which Eleazar's prayer has just recalled (3 Maccabees 6:5). Unusually, the rescued people do not see their rescuers, the reverse of Elisha's servant, whose eyes God opened to see the fiery army (2 Kings 6:17).

3 Maccabees ends with a festival that follows the pattern of Purim. After their rescue the Jews of Egypt feast for seven days, "until the fourteenth" (3 Maccabees 6:40), and fix the days "to be kept as days of joy" for all generations (3 Maccabees 6:36), and again at Ptolemais (3 Maccabees 7:19). Like Esther the book has two royal letters, of death and of rescue (3 Maccabees 3:12–29; 7:1–9), as Greek Esther does in Additions B and E. Its dates are Egyptian, from Pachon to Epiphi (3 Maccabees 6:38). Josephus reports that the Jews of Alexandria kept a festival for a rescue from elephants (Against Apion 2.55).

Eleazar's prayer in 3 Maccabees 6:2–15 asks God to act now as he acted before: against Pharaoh at the sea, against Sennacherib, for the three in the furnace, for Daniel among the lions, and for Jonah in the sea monster. It confesses that the people may have sinned and asks God to punish them himself rather than let the Gentiles mock him (3 Maccabees 6:10–11). The same method shapes the Jewish prayers for fast days: "He Who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah" will answer us (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:4). In Egypt the Jews' meeting house was itself called proseuchē, "prayer," and the book ends with the founding of one (3 Maccabees 7:20; compare Acts 16:13).

sections.h: The Jews of Ptolemaic Egypt in 3 Maccabees
sections.b: 3 Maccabees 4–7 shows the Jews of Egypt as a people spread through the countryside and Alexandria, shipped down the Nile to the river port of Schedia (3 Maccabees 4:9–11) and held in the hippodrome outside the city. The king himself admits that they "have faithfully held the strongholds of our country" (3 Maccabees 6:25), and the Letter of Aristeas says the first Ptolemy settled Jewish soldiers "in garrisons in the country districts" (Letter of Aristeas 13). The book dates its events by Egyptian months (3 Maccabees 6:38), and its rescued people call themselves resident aliens in Egypt (3 Maccabees 6:36; 7:19).

3 Maccabees 6:8 names Jonah last among God's rescues: "wasting away in the belly of the sea monster bred in the deep," he was "shown unharmed to all his own people." The word for the creature, kētos, is the one in Matthew 12:40. The return to his people goes beyond the book of Jonah, which ends the rescue on the dry land (Jonah 2:10).

Eleazar recalls that Daniel was thrown to the lions "because of jealous slander" and brought up "into the light unhurt" (3 Maccabees 6:7; compare Daniel 6:4, 22–23). The Jews of Egypt, slandered by courtiers and set before beasts, saw themselves in him.

sections.h: The three in the furnace in 3 Maccabees
sections.b: 3 Maccabees 6:6 recalls "the three companions in Babylonia" who gave their lives to the fire rather than worship idols. God "made the red-hot furnace wet with dew," a detail from the Greek Daniel (Greek Daniel 3:50), not the Aramaic text, which has the hair of their heads unscorched (Daniel 3:27). Codex Venetus of 3 Maccabees lacks the dew.

3 Maccabees calls the Jews' life in Egypt an apoikia, "settlement abroad" (3 Maccabees 6:10), and a paroikia, "living as resident aliens" (3 Maccabees 6:36). They keep their festival "for all their time as resident aliens" (3 Maccabees 7:19), the same Greek phrase as 1 Peter 1:17. Eleazar claims the promise of Leviticus 26:44, in its Greek form, for Jews "in the land of their enemies" (3 Maccabees 6:15).

sections.b: At the end of 3 Maccabees the faithful Jews kill more than three hundred Jews who had given up the Law, with the king's leave and no trial, and keep the day with joy (3 Maccabees 7:10–15). The book stands in the line of Phinehas (Numbers 25:7–8) and Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2:24–26), but it lacks the inquiry the Law required (Deuteronomy 13:14), and the New Testament rules such killing out (Luke 9:54–55; Romans 12:19).

3 Maccabees sums up apostasy as a matter of food: the renegades "had broken the commands of God for the sake of their stomachs" (3 Maccabees 7:11), and the faithful are those who kept apart "in the matter of food" (3 Maccabees 3:4). Compare 1 Maccabees 1:62–63 and Paul's "Their god is the belly" (Philippians 3:19).

3 Maccabees 4–7 reads like a Greek Esther set in Egypt. The decree spreads mourning "wherever" it arrives (3 Maccabees 4:1–2; Esther 4:3), the king's sleep is the turning point (3 Maccabees 5:11; Esther 6:1, in reverse), a second royal letter blames the king's advisers and calls the Jews God's sons (3 Maccabees 7:1–9; Greek Esther's Addition E, after Esther 8:12), three hundred are killed (3 Maccabees 7:15; Esther 9:15), and a festival is fixed for the generations (3 Maccabees 6:36; Esther 9:27–28). Unlike Hebrew Esther, 3 Maccabees names God on every page and ends with an open miracle.
